usamts-2015-r2-01.title: Deduction
usamts-2015-r2-01.body:
Write $(r,c)$ for the square in row $r$ (from the top) and column $c$ (from the left). The length of the shortest path between two squares is $|r_1-r_2|+|c_1-c_2|$. By (i), every row ends up with exactly 4 numbers and every column with exactly 3.

**The 12's and the 10.** The only pairs of squares at distance $5+7=12$ are the two pairs of opposite corners. The only square at distance 10 from the given 10 at $(2,2)$ is $(6,8)$ (we need $|r-2|\le 4$ and $|c-2|\le 6$ to add up to 10). So $(6,8)=10$, and the 12's go in the other two corners $(1,8)$ and $(6,1)$.

**The 11's.** Two squares at distance 11 differ by $5$ rows and $6$ columns, or by $4$ rows and $7$ columns; either way one of them is a corner. The only free corner is $(1,1)$, so one 11 is there, and the other is at $(6,7)$ or $(5,8)$. Column 8 already holds $12, 8, 10$, so the 11 is at $(6,7)$. Row 6 now holds $12,3,11,10$ and is full.

**The 7, 8, 9.** The squares at distance 7 from the 7 at $(5,6)$ that are still allowed are $(3,1)$ and $(1,3)$. The second 8 (distance 8 from $(3,8)$) can only go in $(4,1)$, $(6,3)$ or $(5,2)$, and $(6,3)$ is excluded because row 6 is full. The second 9 (distance 9 from $(5,7)$) can only go in $(2,1)$ or $(1,2)$. So the 8 and the 9 both go in columns 1 and 2, which together already contain 11, 12, 10, 5; after placing them, columns 1 and 2 hold 3 numbers each. Hence the 7 cannot go in column 1, so $(1,3)=7$. Row 1 is now full ($11,7,6,12$), so the 9 is at $(2,1)$; column 1 is then full, so the 8 is at $(5,2)$.

**The rest.** The second 6 (distance 6 from $(1,5)$) is forced to $(5,3)$, which fills row 5 ($8,6,7,9$). Column 3 is now full ($7,1,6$), so the second 1, which must be next to $(2,3)$, is at $(2,4)$; this fills row 2 ($9,10,1,1$). The numbers still to place are a 5, a 3 and two 4's. Columns 1, 2, 3, 5 and 8 are full, so the two missing numbers of row 3 go in $(3,6)$ and $(3,7)$. Neither is at distance 3 from the 3 at $(6,5)$, and the two 4's cannot both be there, so these squares hold the 5 and one 4. The 5 must be at distance 5 from $(4,2)$, so $(3,6)=5$ and $(3,7)=4$. Column 7 is now full, so the last two numbers go in $(4,4)$ and $(4,6)$; the 4 needs distance 4 from $(3,7)$, so $(4,4)=4$ and $(4,6)=3$.

**Check.** Rows contain 4 numbers each and columns 3 each. Distances: 1's $(2,3),(2,4)$: 1; 2's $(3,4),(4,5)$: 2; 3's $(4,6),(6,5)$: 3; 4's $(3,7),(4,4)$: 4; 5's $(3,6),(4,2)$: 5; 6's $(1,5),(5,3)$: 6; 7's $(1,3),(5,6)$: 7; 8's $(3,8),(5,2)$: 8; 9's $(2,1),(5,7)$: 9; 10's $(2,2),(6,8)$: 10; 11's $(1,1),(6,7)$: 11; 12's $(1,8),(6,1)$: 12. Every step above was forced, so this is the only solution.

usamts-2015-r2-02.title: Construction
usamts-2015-r2-02.body:
Take a unit cube and a square pyramid all of whose edges have length 1 (its four lateral faces are equilateral triangles). Gluing such a pyramid onto a face of the cube removes that square face and adds four triangles. Glue pyramids onto two faces of the cube:

- **Polyhedron $A$:** pyramids on two opposite faces (top and bottom);
- **Polyhedron $B$:** pyramids on two adjacent faces (top and front).

These are not congruent: in $A$ each of the four square faces shares an edge with exactly two other square faces, while in $B$ the back face shares edges with three square faces (left, bottom, right). Each has 4 square faces and 8 triangular faces.

**The piece.** Let $T$ be the planar shape formed by two unit squares sharing a side (a domino, drawn vertically), together with a fan of four equilateral triangles: one triangle sits on the outer vertical side of the **upper** square, and the other three triangles follow around the common apex of the fan, each sharing a side with the previous one. (The four triangles of a fan are exactly the lateral faces of one pyramid, unrolled around its apex.) Let $T'$ be the mirror image of $T$, which is the same as $T$ rotated by $180^\circ$ (fan on the outer side of the **lower** square). The cut-out pieces of both nets below are $T$ and $T'$.

What we need for a polyhedron is a split of its faces into two groups, each group consisting of two adjacent squares $P$, $Q$ plus the four triangles of one pyramid whose (removed) base face is adjacent to $P$ along an edge perpendicular to the edge $PQ$. Then the fan of that pyramid can be unfolded hinged on that edge of $P$, giving a copy of $T$ (or $T'$), and the two groups are joined along one more common edge to form a net.

**Polyhedron $A$** (pyramids on top and bottom; squares front $F$, right $R$, back $K$, left $L$). Group 1: squares $F, R$ with the top fan hinged on the top edge of $F$. Group 2: squares $K, L$ with the bottom fan hinged on the bottom edge of $L$. Laying the belt $F, R, K, L$ out in a row with the top fan above $F$ and the bottom fan below $L$ gives a net of $A$; cutting it along the edge $RK$ yields the two pieces. (The top edge of $F$ is perpendicular to the edge $FR$, and the bottom edge of $L$ to the edge $KL$.)

**Polyhedron $B$** (pyramids on top and front; squares left $L$, back $K$, bottom $D$, right $R$). The top face is adjacent to both $L$ and $K$, and the front face is adjacent to both $D$ and $R$. Group 1: squares $L, K$ with the top fan hinged on the top edge of $L$ (perpendicular to the edge $LK$). Group 2: squares $R, D$ with the front fan hinged on the front edge of $D$ (perpendicular to the edge $RD$). The two groups are joined along the common edge of $K$ and $D$ (the back bottom edge of the cube), which unfolds to a net of $B$; cutting along that edge yields the two pieces.

In both cases each piece is a domino with a fan of four triangles attached to a long side of one end square, and the fan can be unrolled in the same direction in both cases, so the two pieces from $A$ and the two pieces from $B$ are the same pair $T$, $T'$ (up to rotation and reflection). Hence two distinct polyhedra can produce the same two pieces.

usamts-2015-r2-03.title: Induction on tail sums
usamts-2015-r2-03.body:
Fix $n$ and write
$$a_k = \frac{k\cdot k!\binom{n}{k}}{n^k} = \frac{k\cdot n!}{(n-k)!\,n^k}.$$
For $0\le r\le n-1$ let $S_r = a_{n-r} + a_{n-r+1} + \cdots + a_n$ be the sum of the last $r+1$ terms. We claim
$$S_r = \frac{n!}{r!\,n^{\,n-r-1}}.$$

For $r=0$: $S_0 = a_n = \dfrac{n\cdot n!}{n^n} = \dfrac{n!}{0!\,n^{n-1}}$.

If the claim holds for $r = m-1$ (where $1\le m\le n-1$), then
$$S_m = S_{m-1} + a_{n-m} = \frac{n!}{(m-1)!\,n^{n-m}} + \frac{(n-m)\,n!}{m!\,n^{n-m}} = \frac{n!\,\big(m + (n-m)\big)}{m!\,n^{n-m}} = \frac{n!}{m!\,n^{\,n-m-1}}.$$

Taking $r = n-1$ gives $\sum_{k=1}^n a_k = S_{n-1} = \dfrac{n!}{(n-1)!\,n^0} = n$, and dividing by $n$ gives the identity.

usamts-2015-r2-03.title: Probability
usamts-2015-r2-03.body:
Roll a fair $n$-sided die repeatedly until some number appears for the second time.

The first $k$ rolls are all distinct in $k!\binom nk$ of the $n^k$ equally likely sequences (choose which $k$ values appear, then their order). Given that, the $(k+1)$st roll repeats one of them with probability $\frac kn$. So the probability that the first repeat happens on roll $k+1$ is
$$\frac kn\cdot\frac{k!\binom nk}{n^k} = \frac{k\cdot k!\binom nk}{n^{k+1}}.$$
These events for $k=1,\ldots,n$ are disjoint, and one of them must occur, because by the pigeonhole principle $n+1$ rolls of an $n$-sided die always contain a repeat. Hence
$$\sum_{k=1}^n \frac{k\cdot k!\binom nk}{n^{k+1}} = 1,$$
which is the required identity after taking a factor $\frac1n$ out of the sum.

usamts-2015-r2-04.title: Comparing leading terms
usamts-2015-r2-04.body:
**These work.** If $P(x) = c$ then $P(a+b)-P(b) = 0$, a multiple of $c$. If $P(x)=cx$ then $P(a+b)-P(b) = ca = P(a)$.

**No others.** Suppose $P$ works and $\deg P = d \ge 1$. Fix an integer $b$ and let
$$H(x) = P(x+b) - P(b), \qquad r(x) = H(x) - P(x).$$
$H$ has the same degree $d$ and the same leading coefficient as $P$, so $\deg r < d$ (or $r = 0$). For every integer $a$, $P(a)$ divides $H(a)$ and $P(a)$, hence divides $r(a)$. Since $\deg r < \deg P$, we have $|r(a)| < |P(a)|$ for all sufficiently large integers $a$, and a multiple of $P(a)$ smaller in absolute value than $P(a)$ must be $0$. So $r(a) = 0$ for infinitely many $a$, and the polynomial $r$ is identically zero. Therefore
$$P(x+b) = P(x) + P(b) \quad\text{for all } x \text{ and all integers } b.$$

Taking $x = b = 0$ gives $P(0) = 2P(0)$, so $P(0)=0$. Taking $b=1$ gives $P(x+1) = P(x) + P(1)$, so by induction $P(k) = kP(1)$ for every positive integer $k$. The polynomials $P(x)$ and $P(1)\,x$ agree at infinitely many points, so $P(x) = cx$ with $c = P(1)$, an integer.

Hence the solutions are the constant polynomials $P(x)=c$ and the linear polynomials $P(x)=cx$, $c\in\mathbb Z$.

usamts-2015-r2-05.title: Lower bound and construction
usamts-2015-r2-05.body:
Write $n = 2k$; we show the minimum is $6k^2 - 2 = \frac32 n^2 - 2$.

Place the grid with corners at $(0,0)$ and $(4k,4k)$. The blocks are $[2a,2a+2]\times[2b,2b+2]$. Call the $(2k+1)^2$ lattice points with both coordinates even the **block corners**. Every unit square $[x,x+1]\times[y,y+1]$ has exactly one corner with both coordinates even; call it $\varphi$ of the square. It is a corner of the block containing the square, and the four squares of a block are sent by $\varphi$ to the four different corners of that block.

**Lemma.** In a $(2k+1)\times(2k+1)$ grid of cells, let $U$ be a set of $s$ cells, connected through shared sides, such that every $2\times 2$ subgrid contains a cell of $U$. Then $s \ge 2k^2 - 1$.

*Proof.* The $(2k)^2$ interior lattice points of this grid are each the center of a $2\times 2$ subgrid, so each is a corner of some cell of $U$. Order the cells of $U$ so that each cell after the first shares a side with an earlier one (possible because $U$ is connected). The first cell has 4 corners, and each later cell shares a side, hence two corners, with an earlier cell, so it contributes at most 2 new corners. Thus the cells of $U$ have at most $4 + 2(s-1) = 2s+2$ corners in total, and $2s+2 \ge 4k^2$. $\blacksquare$

**Lower bound.** Let $S$ satisfy (i) and (ii), and let $V = \varphi(S)$, a set of block corners. Think of the block corners as the cells of a $(2k+1)\times(2k+1)$ grid (two block corners are adjacent if they differ by 2 in one coordinate). The four corners of a block form a $2\times 2$ subgrid, and by (ii) the block contains a square of $S$, whose $\varphi$ is one of these corners; so every $2\times2$ subgrid meets $V$.

If two squares of $S$ share a side and lie in **different** blocks, they have the same $\varphi$ (the shared side lies on a block boundary line, and both squares touch the same even–even endpoint of it). If they share a side and lie in the **same** block, their $\varphi$'s are two adjacent corners of that block; join these two corners by an edge, forming a graph $G$ on $V$. Walking along a side-connected chain of squares of $S$ (property (i)), $\varphi$ either stays put or moves along an edge of $G$, so $G$ is connected. In particular $V$ is connected as a set of cells, and the lemma gives $|V| \ge 2k^2 - 1$.

Choose a spanning tree of $G$; it has $|V| - 1 \ge 2k^2 - 2$ edges. Each tree edge comes from a pair of squares of $S$ in one block; assign the edge to that block (choosing one block if there are several). Suppose a block gets $t$ tree edges. These edges join corners of this block and contain no cycle, so they touch at least $t+1$ distinct corners, and each of those corners is $\varphi$ of a different square of $S$ in this block. So the block contains at least $t+1$ squares of $S$, and at least 1 if $t=0$ by (ii). Summing over the $4k^2$ blocks,
$$|S| \ge 4k^2 + (2k^2 - 2) = 6k^2 - 2.$$

**Construction.** Number the rows and columns $1$ to $4k$ and write $(i,j)$ for row $i$, column $j$. Shade:

- the $4k-2$ squares $(i,2)$ for $2 \le i \le 4k-1$;
- for each $m = 1, \ldots, k$, the $4k-3$ squares $(4m-1, j)$ for $3 \le j \le 4k-1$;
- for each $m = 1, \ldots, k$, the $2k-1$ squares $(4m-2, j)$ for $j = 3, 5, 7, \ldots, 4k-1$.

The total is $(4k-2) + k(4k-3) + k(2k-1) = 6k^2 - 2$. It is connected: the rows $4m-1$ hang off column 2, and each square $(4m-2, j)$ sits directly above $(4m-1, j)$. Every block is hit: the blocks in rows $4m-3, 4m-2$ meet row $4m-2$, which contains $(4m-2,2)$ and a square in each pair of columns $\{3,4\},\{5,6\},\ldots,\{4k-1,4k\}$; the blocks in rows $4m-1, 4m$ meet row $4m-1$, which contains columns $2, 3, \ldots, 4k-1$. (For $k=1$ this is the central $2\times 2$ square of the $4\times 4$ grid.)

Hence the minimum is $6k^2 - 2 = \frac32 n^2 - 2$.

*Note.* The official solution's text describes the last family of squares with a misprinted formula; the description above matches the official diagram and was checked by computer for $k = 1, \ldots, 5$.
